course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
title: Determinants and Invertibility
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
sessionGoal: Students should be able to compute determinants, use determinant properties, and decide when a matrix is invertible.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start with: determinant zero means the matrix collapses space and is not invertible.
Write: \(\det(A)\) nonzero means invertible for square matrices.
sayThisFirst: The determinant is a number attached to a square matrix.
For a 2D matrix, determinant tells area scaling and orientation.
For a square matrix, determinant nonzero means invertible.
Determinant zero means the columns are dependent.
Row swaps, row scaling, and row replacement affect determinants in different ways.
boardPlan: Write the invertible matrix test: \(\det(A)\neq 0\) means invertible.
Problem 1: compute a 3 by 3 determinant using expansion or row reduction.
Problem 2: track determinant changes from row operations.
Problem 3: find the k value that makes determinant zero.

keyFormulas.name: Invertibility test
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: Nonzero determinant means the matrix has an inverse.

keyFormulas.name: Row swap
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: A row swap multiplies determinant by -1.

keyFormulas.name: Row scaling
keyFormulas.latex: R_i\leftarrow cR_i \Rightarrow \det \text{ is multiplied by } c
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: Scaling a row scales the determinant.

keyFormulas.name: Row replacement
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: Adding a multiple of one row to another does not change determinant.

commonMistakes: Using determinant tests on non-square matrices.
Forgetting that row replacement does not change the determinant.
Forgetting that a row swap changes the sign.
Saying determinant zero means no solutions for every Ax=b. More precisely, it means A is not invertible.
Dropping a negative sign during cofactor expansion.
notationWarnings: Use \det(A), not |A| if students may confuse it with absolute value.
For parameter problems, write \det(A(k))=0 to find non-invertible values.
Always mention square matrix before saying determinant/invertible.

problems.title: Compute a determinant and decide invertibility
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: determinant is just a number. For a square matrix, nonzero means invertible.

drawInstructions: Write the 3 by 3 matrix large on the board.
Choose the first row for cofactor expansion because it has a zero.
Circle the zero entry to show why that term disappears.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the minus sign on the middle cofactor.
Saying invertible only because the matrix is 3 by 3. It is invertible because det is nonzero.

problems.title: Track determinant changes from row operations
problems.studentPromptLatex:
Suppose \(A\) is a \(3\times 3\) matrix with \(\det(A)=4\). A matrix \(B\) is made from \(A\) by doing these row operations in order:
1. Swap rows 1 and 2.
2. Multiply row 3 by 5.
3. Replace row 1 by row 1 plus 2 times row 2.
Find \(\det(B)\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: do not try to invent A. Just track what each row operation does to the determinant.

drawInstructions: Label row replacement as no change.

walkthrough.label: Apply the row swap
walkthrough.latex:
Swapping two rows multiplies the determinant by \(-1\):
\[4\mapsto -4.\]

walkthrough.label: Apply row scaling
walkthrough.latex:
Multiplying one row by 5 multiplies the determinant by 5:
\[-4\mapsto -20.\]

walkthrough.label: Apply row replacement
walkthrough.latex: Replacing a row by itself plus a multiple of another row does not change the determinant. So it stays \(-20\).

commonMistakes: Thinking row replacement changes the determinant.
Forgetting row swap changes the sign.
Multiplying by 5 three times instead of once. Only one row was scaled.

problems.title: Find when a matrix is invertible
problems.studentPromptLatex:
For what values of \(k\) is
\[A(k)=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&k\\0&1&3\\2&0&1\end{bmatrix}\]
invertible?
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: invertible means determinant nonzero. So find \(\det(A(k))\), set it not equal to zero.

drawInstructions: After computing 13-2k, draw a number line and mark k=13/2 as the bad value.
Say: every other value is okay.

walkthrough.label: Use determinant test
walkthrough.latex: A square matrix \(A\) is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero: \(\det(A)\neq 0\).

walkthrough.label: Compute the determinant
walkthrough.latex:
Expand along the second row or compute directly:
\[\det(A(k))=13-2k.\]

walkthrough.label: Find the bad value
walkthrough.latex:
The matrix is not invertible when
\[13-2k=0.\]
So \(2k=13\), and \(k=\frac{13}{2}\).

walkthrough.label: State the invertible values
walkthrough.latex: Therefore, \(A(k)\) is invertible for every \(k\) except \(\frac{13}{2}\).

commonMistakes: Giving the non-invertible value when the question asks for invertible values.
Forgetting to say k not equal to 13/2.
Setting determinant equal to 1 instead of nonzero.

practiceLabPointer.note: More parameter determinant problems are in Section 4.

wrapUpQuestions: What determinant value means not invertible?
Which row operation does not change determinant?
What does a row swap do to determinant?
For parameter problems, what equation finds the bad values?

linksToWebsite.label: Practice Lab Section 4

qualityControlNotes: Problem 3 checked: det(A(k))=13-2k, so non-invertible when k=13/2.

open.title: One number that tells you if you can undo a matrix
say: Last time a matrix moved space around. Today: one number, the determinant, tells you how much it stretches area, whether it flips things over, and whether you can undo it.
If you remember one line from today: determinant zero means not invertible.

ask.q: A transformation squashes the whole plane onto a line. Can you undo it?
ask.a: No. Many points land on the same spot, so there's no way to know where they came from.

idea.title: The determinant is the area (or volume) scale factor
say: Take the unit square and hit it with A. It becomes a parallelogram. The determinant is that parallelogram's area, with a minus sign if the square got flipped over.
If the determinant is 0, the square got flattened to a line: area zero, information lost, no inverse.
In 3D the same story holds for volume: the unit cube becomes a slanted box whose volume is |det A|.
draw: Draw the unit square and, next to it, a parallelogram labeled 'area = |det A|'.
Draw a second parallelogram squashed flat onto a line: 'det A = 0, not invertible'.
Draw a mirrored version: 'det A < 0, orientation flips'.

ask.q: A has det 3. What happens to the area of a shape with area 2 after applying A?
Why does det = 0 mean the columns are dependent?
ask.a: The parallelogram they span is flat, so the columns lie on one line (or one plane in 3D).

launch.say: Compute det A and decide whether A is invertible. Look for a row or column that makes expansion easy.
circulate: Watch the middle cofactor's sign: it's minus.
Who picked a row with a zero? That saves a whole 2 × 2 determinant.

askFirst.q: Which row or column would you expand along, and why?
askFirst.a: Row 1 (or column 1), because it has a zero, so one term disappears.

steps.say: Expand along row 1. Signs alternate: plus, minus, plus. The zero kills the third term.

ask.q: What's the sign pattern for a 3 × 3?
ask.a: + − + on the first row, alternating like a checkerboard.

ask.q: Which entries do you cross out to get the first minor?
The answer is negative. Is that a problem?
ask.a: No. It just means A flips orientation; the volume scale is 15.

ask.q: What does det A = −15 say about the unit cube?
ask.a: It becomes a box of volume 15, mirrored.

si08-p1.meaning: A stretches volume by a factor of 15 and turns the cube inside-out. Nothing gets flattened, so every output comes from exactly one input and A can be undone.

ifStuck.then: check the middle cofactor's sign: it's −1 · det(minor), not +1.

si08-p1.transition: We computed from scratch. Next: predict the determinant after row operations without knowing the matrix at all.

launch.say: We don't know A, only that det A = 4. After three row operations, what's det B?
circulate: Nobody should be inventing a matrix. Just track the effect of each operation.
Check the replacement step: it changes nothing.

askFirst.q: What does each type of row operation do to the determinant?
askFirst.a: Swap: multiply by −1. Scale a row by c: multiply by c. Add a multiple of a row: no change.

ask.q: Why can we solve this without knowing A?
ask.a: Each row operation changes the determinant by a known factor.

steps.say: A swap flips the sign: 4 becomes −4.

ask.a: Swapping two rows reverses orientation, like looking in a mirror.

steps.say: Scaling one row by 5 multiplies the determinant by 5: −4 becomes −20.

ask.q: What if we scaled all three rows by 5?
ask.a: Then det gets multiplied by 5³ = 125, which is why det(5A) = 125 det A for a 3 × 3.

steps.why: Scaling one row stretches the box in one direction only. That's the difference between det(5A) and scaling a single row.

steps.say: Row replacement doesn't change the determinant. det B = −20.

ask.q: Why doesn't adding a multiple of a row change the volume?
ask.a: It's a shear: it slides the box sideways, which doesn't change its volume.

si08-p2.meaning: Row operations change the determinant in predictable ways: swaps flip the sign, scaling multiplies, and shears (replacements) leave it alone. That's also why row reducing is a fast way to compute determinants.

ifStuck.if: a student multiplies by 5 three times
ifStuck.then: ask how many rows were scaled. Only row 3.

si08-p2.transition: Last one: find the value of k that makes the determinant zero, the one bad value.

launch.say: For which k is A(k) invertible? Find the determinant as a function of k.
circulate: Is anyone setting det = 1? Invertible means det ≠ 0.
Check the final answer is the invertible values, not the bad one.

askFirst.q: What equation finds the bad values of k?

steps.say: Invertible exactly when the determinant is nonzero.

ask.q: What are we actually solving for, then?
ask.a: The k values where det = 0; every other k is fine.

ask.q: Why does k only appear once?
ask.a: It's a single entry, so the determinant is linear in k.

ask.q: What happens to the columns at k = 13/2?
ask.a: They become dependent and the box goes flat.

ask.q: How should you phrase the final answer?
ask.a: k ≠ 13/2. The question asks where A(k) IS invertible.

steps.why: Read the question: answering with the bad value instead of the good ones costs points.

si08-p3.meaning: As k changes, the third column swings around. At exactly k = 13/2 it lands in the plane of the other two columns, and the volume collapses to zero.

ifStuck.then: reread the question together: it asks for the invertible values.

wrap.write: det ≠ 0 ⟺ invertible. Swap: ×(−1). Scale a row by c: ×c. Replace (add a multiple): no change.

exit.q: What determinant value means not invertible?
Which row operation doesn't change the determinant?
exit.a: Adding a multiple of one row to another.

exit.q: What is det(3A) for a 3 × 3 matrix with det A = 2?
